title: Changes in flight paths of large-bodied birds after construction of large terrestrial wind turbines
abstract: The proliferation of ever-larger wind turbines poses risks to wildlife, especially from avian collision, yet avoidance behaviour of large-bodied, long-lived bird species in relation to wind turbines remains little studied away from collision “black spots” and offshore marine environments. Here, three-dimensional flight trajectory data are reported from a laser range-finder study of local movements of large-bodied birds (e.g. swans, geese, gulls, cormorants, raptors and cranes, whose populations are relatively more demographically sensitive to collision mortality) in relation to seven terrestrial 150-222 m high (mean 182 m) wind turbines constructed in Denmark in a N-S line. Comparisons of two-dimensional flight passages between turbines pre- (n = 287) and post-construction (n = 1210) showed significant (P < 0.0001) reductions from 48% to 35% within 150 m of each turbine, with corresponding increase 200-300 m from turbines. Results also showed a significant (P < 0.001) 50% reduction in the percentage of avian passages (from 21% to 10%) through the maximum turbine sweep area after construction and that the proportion of birds that passed between turbines at heights below (0-45 m) and above the turbine sweep area (> 182 m) were significantly greater (P < 0.0001) post-construction than prior to construction. These are the first results from tracking large-bodied bird flight trajectories to show the magnitude of their vertical and horizontal adjustments to the presence of turbines, which have implications for assumptions of even flight densities made by collision risk models currently used to predict avian turbine collision rates.

## **1. Introduction**

Over 341,000 wind turbines (most constructed on land) contributed 3.7% of total global electricity consumption, while moderating climate change, by the end of 2016 (http://www.gwec.net/global-figures/win d-in-numbers/). Increasing numbers of ever-larger wind turbines proliferate risks posed to wildlife, especially from avian collision with the infrastructure, but particularly the rotating blades (Fox et al. 2006). Despite this, avoidance behaviour of large-bodied, long-lived bird species in relation to wind turbines remains little studied away from collision “black spots” (Dahl et al., 2012; Carrete et al., 2012) and offshore marine environments (Desholm and Kahlert 2005). There is no doubt that longer-lived, large-bodied birds, such as swans _Cygnus_ spp., geese _Anser_ and _Branta_ spp., gulls (Laridae), Great Cormorants _Phalacrocorax carbo_ , diurnal birds of prey and Common Crane _Grus grus_ , are relatively more demographically sensitive to collision mortality than smaller avian species subject to lower annual survival rates (Desholm 2009). Earlier

studies showed that migrating waterbirds can show large scale avoidance of marine wind farms (Desholm and Kahlert 2005; Plonczkier and Simms 2012 ) and among those flying within such farms (mainly Common Eider _Somateria mollissima_ which anyway fly low over the sea) showed major flight displacement responses, flying more often equidistant between turbines (Desholm and Kahlert 2005). Despite this, there have been virtually no reported studies of the vertical and horizontal displacement shown by comparing the pre-construction flight trajectories of birds with those post-construction at terrestrial wind turbines. For this reason, we here report differences in the pre-and post-construction three-dimensional flight trajectory data from the first reported laser range-finder study of local movements of large bodied birds in relation to seven terrestrial 150–222 m high (mean 182 m) wind turbines built at a test centre in northern Jutland, Denmark.

## _2.2. Tracking birds in three-dimensional space_

The Østerild wind turbine test centre is located in Østerild Plantation (57[◦] 02[′] N 8[◦] 53[′] W, see Electronic Supplementary Material, Fig. S1), in northwest Jutland, Denmark. The test centre was built within a matrix of conifer plantations, heathland and grazed farmland, situated close to extensive wetlands protected as European Union Special Protection Areas (SPAs), designated for their rare and vulnerable breeding and regularly occurring staging migratory species under the EU Birds Directive (Therkildsen and Elmeros 2015; 2017; Supplementary Material Fig. S1). Observations were carried out prior to construction of any – turbines at the site during 2011 2012 to compare with observations carried out post-construction during 2013–2016. In the post-construction phase of the project, the wind turbine test centre supported seven turbines designed for deployment offshore in marine environments, which were constructed at 600 m intervals with rotors that reached from 30 m to 222 m above the ground (for full details see Supplementary Material Table S1). Full details of the turbines and their circumstances can be found in earlier reports from the work available

We tracked birds using a Vectornix Vector 21 Aero laser range finder (range 12 km with 5 m range accuracy over this distance) to measure instantaneous flight altitude, angle and distance from an observer positioned between the turbines. Sequential measurements of the same bird/flock returning the exact geographical location of each measurement were used to plot the movement in three-dimensional space. The device is hand-held and was highly effective at tracking large-bodied birds/flocks up to 4 km range. The study area did not constitute a migration area for long distance migrants, so most movements represented the local movements between foraging areas of individual birds, which therefore had prior knowledge of the turbines. Sequential data on altitude, distance and angle to a bird/flock from the point of detection to the point at which they could no longer be followed were then entered into a GIS platform (ARCMap 10). For each bird/flock trajectory path passing between adjacent turbines, the distance to the wind turbine to either side was measured, as well as the flight altitude, when crossing the line connecting adjacent wind turbines. ## _2.3. Statistical analysis_

The precise flight altitude at which each individual observed track crossed the line of wind turbines was determined. Altitudes were – grouped in three classes: below (0 45m), within rotor sweep area (45–182 m) and those above ( _>_ 182 m) based on the average upper and lower height of the sweep area for each individual turbine (because these varied, see electronic Supplementary Material Table S1). There were too few observations (two, compared to 49 observations postconstruction) at altitudes higher than 182 m to evaluate differences between pre- and post-construction. Therefore only _<_ 45 m and 45–182 m altitude intervals were used in the main analysis, although we consider the increase in frequency of passage above 182 m to likely reflect a secondary avoidance effect of birds climbing to avoid the rotors. The distance classes from the point at which birds/flocks crossed the line between adjacent turbines were combined into 50 m distance classes from the nearest wind turbine to the north or south. Our model included altitude class, horizontal distances to nearest turbine and pre-/postconstruction context, together with number of observations in each as the response variable. Multiway frequency analysis (Tabachnick and Fidell 2013, which allows relationships between discrete variables to be investigated using a log-linear analytical framework) was used to test for vertical and horizontal avoidance behaviour post-construction relative to the baseline observations before the turbines were erected using Proc catmod in SAS 9.3 (SasInstitute, Cary, NC).

We compared the cumulated height and distance of all bird passages registered pre- and post-construction as shown in Fig. 1B. Although during the pre-construction phase there were no rotors present, in the two-dimensional space where the rotors were subsequently positioned were described and the proportion of passages through (a) the sweep area of the largest turbine and (b) the sweep area of the average turbine compared pre- and post-construction using a χ[2 ] test. Because more bird passages were witnessed _>_ 222 m height (the top of the sweep zone of the highest turbine) during the post-construction phase than prior to wind turbine construction (see Fig. 1B), we also tested these proportions only among passages recorded below 222 m. Throughout these analyses, it was assumed that the orientation of the wind turbine sweep area was parallel to the north-south line of the wind turbines. In reality, turbine orientation responds to wind direction, as do the birds. This conservative assumption therefore includes, for example, bird passages through the sweep area when blades are perpendicular to the direction of travel and offered no danger to the passing birds.

Birds showed significant differences in flight heights post-construction compared to preconstruction, with 36.6% crossing below 45 m prior to construction compared to 45.1% afterwards, and 62.7% flying within the turbine blade sweep-area level pre-construction compared to 50.9% subsequently. Only nine out of 287 passages of tracked birds pre-construction (0.7%) used airspace above 182 m prior to turbine construction, whereas 4.0% (79 cases) did so post-construction (Fig. 1A). All main factors in the model showed significant interaction effects with period, interaction effects that suggest that birds altered their altitude or their distance in relation to the presence of the wind turbines (Table 1). However, there were no indications that individual flocks changed both altitude and distance, as the interaction between altitude distance and period was not significant.

The proportion of bird passages passing through the sweep area of the largest turbine post-construction (n = 60) was 20.9% compared to 79.1% passing outside (n = 227), which was significantly less (χ[2 ] = 25.0, df = 1, _P <_ 0.001) compared to 10.2% (n = 124) and 89.8% (n = 1096) post-construction. The same calculation for the average sweep areas of the six smaller turbines showed a similar result (n = 34 out of 287, 11.9% _versus_ n = 61 out of 1210, 5.0%, χ[2 ] = 18.4, df = 1, _P <_ 0.001). These proportions were tested only among passages recorded below 222 m and derived similar results (pre-construction: 60 in sweep area, 225 outside, 21.1%; post-construction: 124 in sweep area, 1044 outside, 10.6%; χ[2 ] = 22.56, df = 1, _P <_ 0.001).

## **4. Discussion**

These are the first ever studies of three-dimensional avian movements using laser range finders to compare pre- and post-construction at an onshore windfarm test centre to show such avoidance. The results confirm observations of migrating waterbirds at offshore windfarms (Desholm and Kahlert 2005; Plonczkier and Simms 2012) and migrating raptors at a coastal windfarm (Hull and Muir 2013) that show avoidance behaviour at different spatial scales in response to windfarm construction. These include specifically flying more midway between turbines and less in the air space in close proximity to the sweep areas, although such observations remain rare (Villegas-Patraca et al., 2014). Birds observed in this investigation showed vertical avoidance, reducing the flight frequency when passing between turbines at sweep area altitudes by 12%, increasing flight frequencies above and below sweep area altitudes by a similar amount. Vertical avoidance of wind turbines by flying birds has been reported from Pink-footed Geese _Anser brachyrhynchus_ (Plonczkier and Simms 2012) and other waterbirds at offshore windfarms (Desholm and Kahlert 2005) but not onshore, as in this case, comprising largely local breeding, staging and wintering avian populations.

Probabilities of large-bodied birds flying through the maximum turbine sweep area post-construction was _c_ .50% less than preconstruction, many of which likely did so when the turbine rotors

_O.R. Therkildsen et al._

were stopped or at angles where collision was not a risk. Although the possibility of a change in observer detectability bias pre- and postconstruction cannot be fully eliminated, it would appear that 10% fewer birds flew within the actual sweep area of the turbines and 12% – fewer between the heights of 45 182 m post-construction by flying above and below these altitudes. This was also confirmed by our own post-construction observations of birds climbing up over, or losing height to fly below 45 m. Post-construction, the majority (64.7%) of birds passing between wind turbines did so more than 150 m from the turbines, compared to 50.5% pre-construction, when birds showed a more even distribution (Fig. 1A). Hence, large-bodied birds showed vertical and horizontal avoidance behaviour in response to the construction of turbines.

This study is the first to assess before-after comparisons of largebodied avian flight trajectories in relation to wind turbine construction, adding to the body of evidence that a combination of vertical and horizontal avoidance behaviour in such species undertaking local movements at least partially explains simultaneous observations of extremely low levels of avian collision rates. It must be stressed that this study was at a terrestrial test site comprising one line of unusually large turbines, unlikely to be representative of more typical land-based windfarms that comprise blocks of smaller turbines to which offshore birds react in different ways (Masden et al., 2012). Caution should also be urged in applying such results indiscriminately to avian species at all wind farms as there remains no doubt that collision risk remains highly weather, site and species specific. Nevertheless, at this test site, we contend that the degree of avoidance shown by large-bodied birds in this study likely contributes to the very low levels of avian collision rates suggested by dog searches under these turbines (Therkildsen and Elmeros 2015, 2017). More importantly, vertical and horizontal avoidance results in inequality in avian density and height distribution post-construction, which is used in collision risk models such as that of Band (2012), which would therefore have overestimated collision risk at this site pre-construction.
